report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Knowledge of memory and learning processes may inform teachers' educational decisions.
However, to our knowledge, no psychometrically validated instrument specifically assesses teachers' procedural knowledge of these processes through realistic classroom scenarios.
This Stage 1 Registered Report aims to develop and validate a scenario-based measure of Italian teachers' procedural knowledge of memory and learning processes.
Approximately 600 Italian teachers, from preschool to upper-secondary education, will be recruited through proportional stratified quota sampling based on sex, geographical area, and school level.
Following two pilot studies and iterative revisions, 30 original items were retained and paired with conceptually matched items to create two intended parallel forms.
All participants will complete the 60 multiple-choice items online.
Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses will be conducted separately for each form in independent subsamples.
Measurement invariance across forms will be examined if corresponding factor structures are supported.
Internal consistency will be estimated using Cronbach's alpha.

Mixed-effects logistic regression will examine associations between itemlevel accuracy and teaching experience, educational attainment, and, among teachers with tertiary qualifications, academic field.
We expect interpretable, replicable factor structures and adequate internal consistency, with measurement invariance providing additional evidence of comparability across forms.
Higher accuracy is tentatively expected with higher educational attainment, psycho-pedagogical qualifications, and fewer years of teaching experience.
The study will provide initial evidence on the psychometric properties of the proposed measure.
If the findings support its validity and reliability, the instrument could subsequently be used to identify teachers' knowledge gaps and inform teacher education initiatives.

Assessing teachers' knowledge of memory and learning processes is theoretically and educationally relevant since they constitute the cognitive mechanisms through which students acquire, retain, retrieve, and transfer knowledge.

Research in cognitive and educational psychology has identified several principles that can substantially improve learning, such as retrieval practice, distributed practice, and instructional designs that take into account the limits of working memory and cognitive load (Dunlosky et al., 2013; Kirschner et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Research in cognitive and educational psychology has identified several principles that can substantially improve learning, such as retrieval practice, distributed practice, and instructional designs that take into account the limits of working memory and cognitive load <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dunlosky et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kirschner et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: However, pre-service and in-service teachers do not always possess accurate knowledge of effective learning strategies or memory-related principles and may misjudge the relative effectiveness of different approaches to studying and instruction (Firth, 2021; Halamish, 2018).
text.formatted: However, pre-service and in-service teachers do not always possess accurate knowledge of effective learning strategies or memory-related principles and may misjudge the relative effectiveness of different approaches to studying and instruction <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Firth, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Halamish, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This misjudgment may partly reflect the counterintuitive nature of some evidence-based learning strategies.

Techniques such as retrieval practice, distributed practice, and interleaved practice introduce difficulties that can slow initial learning while improving long-term retention, whereas less effective strategies may produce rapid short-term gains and create powerful illusions of learning (Bjork, 1994; Bjork et al., 2013; Clark & Bjork, 2014).

text.text: Practical classroom experience alone may be insufficient to correct these misconceptions, as teachers' metacognitive knowledge of evidence-based learning strategies does not necessarily improve with years of teaching practice and, in some studies, more experienced teachers have demonstrated less accurate judgments than novices (Firth, 2021; Halamish, 2018).

text.text: Limited coverage during initial teacher education may also contribute to these knowledge gaps.
For example, Surma et al. (2018) found that distributed practice and retrieval practice were often not fully covered in textbooks and syllabi used in Flemish and Dutch teacher education programs.

text.text: Addressing these gaps is important because teachers' professional knowledge is considered a core component of instructional quality and has been linked to student learning outcomes in several domains (Baumert et al., 2010; Kunter et al., 2013; Sadler et al., 2013).

text.text: Measuring teachers' knowledge of memory and learning processes may therefore help to identify strengths and gaps in the knowledge base that informs their educational decisions.
A particularly relevant distinction concerns whether such knowledge is assessed at a declarative or procedural level.

Declarative items typically require respondents to indicate their level of agreement with statements presented in isolation, without reference to a specific classroom context, and therefore focus more directly on explicit knowledge or beliefs.

By contrast, procedural items require teachers to evaluate how they would act in a specific classroom context in order to support students' learning, thereby focusing on how knowledge is applied to educational decision-making and on self-reported behavioral intentions.
This distinction is important because declarative knowledge may be biased by teachers' self image and not always align with how they act or intend to act in educational settings.
Consequently, measures based only on explicit statements may not fully capture the knowledge that guides teachers' classroom decisions.

For this reason, assessing teachers' knowledge through realistic, scenario-based items may provide a more ecologically valid measure of how knowledge about memory and learning processes is applied in educational contexts (Rousseau, 2021; Sullivan et al., 2021; Tovazzi et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For this reason, assessing teachers' knowledge through realistic, scenario-based items may provide a more ecologically valid measure of how knowledge about memory and learning processes is applied in educational contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Rousseau, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Sullivan et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Tovazzi et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Existing research has assessed teachers' general pedagogical or psycho-pedagogical knowledge more broadly (OECD, 2026; Voss et al., 2011), as well as teachers' and instructors' beliefs, metacognitive judgments, or knowledge about specific memory and learning strategies (Firth, 2021; Halamish, 2018; Morehead et al., 2016; Surma et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Existing research has assessed teachers' general pedagogical or psycho-pedagogical knowledge more broadly <ref type="bibr">(OECD, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Voss et al., 2011)</ref>, as well as teachers' and instructors' beliefs, metacognitive judgments, or knowledge about specific memory and learning strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Firth, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Halamish, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Morehead et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Surma et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, to our knowledge no psychometrically validated instrument is currently available to assess teachers' procedural knowledge of memory and learning processes through realistic classroom scenarios.

This gap is important because it hinders investigation of teachers ability to apply evidence-based principles of memory and learning to educational situations that resemble those encountered in classroom practice.
The aim of the present study is therefore to develop and psychometrically validate a measurement scale assessing teachers' procedural knowledge of memory and learning processes.

The scale will consist of scenariobased multiple-choice items describing educational situations that teachers may encounter in their professional practice, organized into two intended parallel forms designed to assess the same underlying aspects of knowledge through conceptually matched but distinct scenarios.
The development of the present scale originated within a broader research program aimed at investigating Italian teachers' adherence to neuromyths.

The main objective of this broader program is to develop measures assessing adherence to neuromyths both when neuromyths are presented as explicit statements and when they are embedded in realistic educational scenarios.

Examining the association between neuromyth adherence and knowledge of memory and learning processes is important for evaluating the construct validity of the neuromyth measures and requires an independently validated measure of teachers' knowledge of memory and learning processes.
The development of the present scale therefore constitutes the first stage of this broader research program.
Importantly, the relevance of the present instrument is not limited to its future use in research on neuromyths.

Teachers' knowledge of memory and learning processes is itself a theoretically and educationally meaningful construct, as it may inform decisions concerning study activities, instructional strategies, feedback, practice, and the organization of learning.

A validated measure of this knowledge can therefore be used independently to identify areas of strength and potential knowledge gaps, investigate differences associated with teachers' education and professional training, and evaluate the effects of interventions intended to improve evidence-based educational knowledge.
Findings on procedural knowledge of memory and learning processes suggest that such knowledge may be associated with several teachers' backgrounds and educational variables.

First, evidence regarding teaching experience is mixed. Halamish (2018) found that in-service teachers' metacognitive knowledge of evidence-based learning strategies did not increase with tenure and was negatively associated with years of teaching experience.

text.text: However, this pattern is not consistently observed, as Firth (2021) found that response accuracy in a vignette-based measure of teachers' beliefs about memory was not correlated with years of teaching experience.

text.text: Second, results from the Teacher Knowledge Survey (OECD, 2026) indicate that teachers' general pedagogical knowledge tends to increase with their level of formal education, although the advantage associated with master's or doctoral degrees is not consistent across countries.

Third, teachers' pathway into the profession may also be relevant: teachers whose first qualification included only subject-specific preparation, with minimal or no pedagogical preparation or practical teacher training, tended to show lower levels of general pedagogical knowledge in several countries (OECD, 2026).

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest that teaching experience, educational attainment, and academic field are relevant external correlates that need to be considered in the validation of the present scale.

Specifically, the study aims to: (a) investigate the latent structure of the two forms through separate exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses; (b) examine measurement invariance across them; (c) examine external validity by means of associations between performance and selected teacher background and educational variables, including years of teaching experience, educational attainment, and academic field, thereby providing validity evidence based on relations with other variables; and (d) assess the internal consistency of the two forms.

text.text: >MATERIAL AND METHODS
text.formatted: <head n="2." >MATERIAL AND METHODS</head>

text.text: The scale was developed through a multi-step process.

First, an initial pool of 34 multiple-choice items was created on the basis of theoretical and applied work on memory, learning, and cognitive processes (Baddeley et al., 2021; Cornoldi et al., 2018; Eysenck & Keane, 2015).
text.formatted: First, an initial pool of 34 multiple-choice items was created on the basis of theoretical and applied work on memory, learning, and cognitive processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Baddeley et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Cornoldi et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Eysenck & Keane, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Items were designed to vary in difficulty and to describe different concrete educational situations that teachers may encounter in their professional practice.
Each item was embedded in a specific classroom-related context to assess procedural knowledge, rather than knowledge expressed through abstract declarative statements.
Each item included one correct answer and three incorrect alternatives, or distractors, which were also contextualized within the scenario.
The initial item pool was then evaluated for clarity by eight independent evaluators recruited without applying any specific educational or professional eligibility criteria.
For each item, the evaluators were asked to indicate whether the item and its response options were sufficiently clear.
When an item was judged to be unclear, they were asked to identify which aspects were difficult to understand and, where possible, to suggest how the item could be improved.
Items were revised based on this feedback to improve clarity.
The revised items were subsequently administered in a first pilot study with 38 pre-service teachers.
Responses were analyzed to examine preliminary item functioning.

Specifically, item difficulty was inspected by identifying items that were particularly difficult, defined as items with accuracy lower than the chance level of 25% given the four response options per item, and items that were too easy, defined as items with 100% accuracy.
The distribution of responses across distractors was also examined to identify alternatives that were rarely selected or clearly less attractive than the others.
On the basis of these results, a second round of item revisions was conducted by the authors.
A second pilot study was then conducted with 48 Italian in-service teachers.
As in the first pilot study, item difficulty and distractor functioning were inspected by examining accuracy levels and the distribution of responses across alternatives.
In addition, exploratory analyses examined associations between overall response accuracy and several teacher characteristics using separate univariate logistic regression models.
Among these analyses, educational attainment and years of teaching experience showed associations in the directions suggested by previous literature (Halamish, 2018; OECD, 2026).

text.text: Given the small pilot sample, the exploratory nature of these analyses, and the substantial overlap among some participant characteristics, these findings were not considered evidence of the scale's validity, but rather preliminary observations to inform about the design of the larger validation study.
The results of the second pilot study informed a final round of item revisions.
Finally, 30 items were selected based on item difficulty, distractor functioning, and the researchers' evaluation of item content and theoretical relevance.

For each selected item, a conceptually parallel item was created, that is, an item intended to assess the same underlying aspect of knowledge through a different but theoretically equivalent scenario.
These parallel items were then evaluated for clarity by a separate group of eight evaluators and refined based on their feedback.
This procedure resulted in a final pool of 60 scenario-based multiple-choice items, organized into 30 conceptually related item pairs.
The item pool is therefore divided into two parallel forms of 30 items, each form containing one item from each pair.
The form comprising the original items will be referred to as the Original form, and the form comprising their conceptually parallel counterparts as the Twin form.
An overview of the construct assessed by each item and the corresponding theoretical source is provided in Supplementary Material 2.
The study will involve ~600 teachers currently working in Italian schools (see Section 2.3, Sample size justification).
Eligible participants will be teachers working at any school level, from preschool to upper-secondary education.

Participants will be recruited using stratified quota sampling with proportional allocation, based on the 2024/25 reference distribution of Italian state-school teachers (N = 942,997; source: the Italian Ministry of Education and Merit's Portale unico dei dati della scuola).

Strata will be defined by crossing sex (female, male), geographical area (Northern Italy, combining North-West and North-East; Central Italy; Southern Italy and Islands), and school level (preschool, primary school, lower-secondary school, upper-secondary school), yielding 24 strata.
Geographical areas will follow the divisions used by the Italian National Institute of Statistics (Istituto nazionale di statistica, 2025).

The unrounded target for each stratum h was calculated as n h * = n N h N , where n is the target sample size of 600, N h is the number of teachers in stratum h, and N is the total reference population.

Integer recruitment quotas were obtained using the largest remainder method (Hamilton method; Balinski & Young, 2001): each stratum was initially assigned the integer part of its unrounded target, and the remaining places were allocated to strata in descending order of their fractional remainders.

text.text: This procedure ensures that the quotas sum to exactly 600.
Each of the three strata comprising male preschool teachers represented less than 0.04% of the total reference population and received a quota of zero after rounding.
The reference population proportions and planned recruitment quotas for each of the 24 strata are reported in Supplementary Material 3.
The target sample size of approximately 600 teachers was determined primarily on the basis of the planned assessment of structural validity, the primary objective of the study.
This target refers to the final analyzable sample.
Incomplete questionnaires are expected to be excluded by the survey provider (Norstat).

The total sample will be randomly divided into two independent subsamples of approximately 300 participants each, with exploratory factor analyses conducted in the first subsample and confirmatory factor analyses in the second (see the Data analysis section for further details).
Because the Original and Twin forms each comprise 30 items and their factor structures will be examined separately, each analysis will involve approximately 10 participants per item.

This sample size exceeds the criterion specified in the COSMIN Risk of Bias Checklist (Mokkink et al., 2018) for a very good sample-size rating in structural validity studies, which requires at least seven participants per item and a minimum of 100 participants.

Data will be collected through an online questionnaire.
Participants will be recruited through Norstat (https://norstat.co/), a professional online panel provider.

text.text: This recruitment strategy was selected to facilitate access to a large and heterogeneous sample of teachers across different geographical areas and school levels, and to allow data collection to be completed efficiently and anonimously.
The study protocol was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano (protocol number UNIBZ_EDU_2026_08).

Before accessing the questionnaire, participants will be presented with an informed consent form describing the aims of the study, the voluntary nature of participation, the anonymous collection and processing of responses, and the possibility of withdrawing from the study at any time before submission.

After acceptance, participants will then be asked to provide information on relevant sociodemographic, educational, and professional characteristics, including age, sex, region of teaching, school level, subject area taught, years of teaching experience, and highest completed educational qualification.
Age and years of teaching experience will be recorded in years.
Region of teaching will be re-coded into the three geographical areas defined above.
Educational attainment will be classified as upper-secondary school diploma or equivalent, bachelor's degree, master's degree or equivalent, or doctoral degree.

Participants with a tertiary qualification will also report the field of study of their highest completed qualification, which will be classified as psycho-pedagogical (psychology, educational sciences, pedagogy, teacher education, or closely related areas) or non-psycho-pedagogical.

Participants will additionally report separate ratings of their perceived knowledge of memory and learning on a scale from 0 to 10, the cumulative number of hours of non-university courses specifically concerning memory and learning processes that they have completed, the approximate number of peer-reviewed scientific articles they have read during the previous 12 months, and, among these, the approximate number specifically concerning memory and learning processes.
The two knowledge ratings, course hours, and both article counts will be treated as separate continuous variables.
Training undertaken as part of a university degree program will not be included in the estimate of non-university course hours.
After completing these background questions, participants will complete the 60 scenariobased items assessing procedural knowledge of memory and learning processes.
The order of all items will be randomized across participants to reduce order effects.
In addition, the order of the response options within each item will be randomized to minimize potential response-position biases.
The questionnaire will be administered in Italian.

The complete questionnaire, including the sociodemographic and professional questions and all items from the Original and Twin forms, is provided in its original Italian version in Supplementary Material 1a and in English translation in Supplementary Material 1b.
The English translation is provided to facilitate understanding of the items and does not constitute a validated English-language version of the scale.
Recruitment will be monitored throughout data collection to meet the predefined quotas for geographical area, school level, and sex.
Data quality will be assessed through Norstat's standard quality-control procedures.
Incomplete questionnaires will not be included in the analytic dataset.
Norstat automatically monitors survey completion times and compares individual response times with the project-specific median.
Responses completed markedly faster than the other responses in the same study may be flagged and excluded, with ambiguous cases additionally reviewed by Norstat's local panel managers.
All analyses will be conducted in R (R Core Team, 2023).

text.text: The 60-item pool comprises the Original and Twin forms, each containing one item from each conceptually related pair.

Because the two items in each pair were deliberately designed to assess the same underlying principle through similar but distinct educational scenarios, responses to paired items may share pair-specific variance beyond that accounted for by the latent factor(s).
Including both members of each pair in the same model could therefore violate the assumption of local independence.
Accordingly, all EFA and CFA analyses described in this section will be conducted separately for the Original and Twin forms.

To investigate the latent structure, the total sample will be randomly split into two independent subsamples, while preserving the stratification of the whole sample in terms of geographical area, sex, and school level.
EFAs will be conducted in the first subsample.
Each retained solution will then be tested through a CFA (Jöreskog, 1969) in the second subsample, thereby cross-validating the structures in an independent group of participants.
text.formatted: Each retained solution will then be tested through a CFA <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Jöreskog, 1969)</ref> in the second subsample, thereby cross-validating the structures in an independent group of participants.

text.text: The consistency of the solutions across forms will be evaluated by comparing the number and substantive interpretation of the retained factors and the loading patterns of corresponding items.

Before conducting these analyses, the factorability of the item correlation matrices will be examined using the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy (KMO; Kaiser, 1970) and Bartlett's test of sphericity.
text.formatted: Before conducting these analyses, the factorability of the item correlation matrices will be examined using the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of sampling adequacy (KMO; <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kaiser, 1970</ref>) and Bartlett's test of sphericity.

text.text: KMO values above .80 will be considered good, whereas values above .70 will be considered acceptable for factor analysis (Kaiser & Rice, 1974).
text.formatted: KMO values above .80 will be considered good, whereas values above .70 will be considered acceptable for factor analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Kaiser & Rice, 1974)</ref>.

text.text: A statistically significant Bartlett's test will be taken as evidence that the correlation matrix is not an identity matrix.

EFA will be used to explore the latent structures and the pattern of relationships between items and latent factor(s), whereas CFA will be used to test the adequacy of the structures identified through EFA.

Because the measure is a maximum-performance measure in which item responses will be coded dichotomously as correct or incorrect, tetrachoric correlations between items will be used as the starting point for EFA and CFA.
The weighted least squares mean-and variance-adjusted estimator (WLSMV) will be used in both EFA and CFA.
The number of factors to be tested will be determined by considering both parallel analysis and inspection of the scree plot.
Candidate solutions will then be compared in terms of model fit, pattern of factor loadings, presence of cross-loadings, and theoretical interpretability.
The final solutions retained for CFA will be selected based on the convergence of these empirical and theoretical criteria.

When multiple factors are extracted, an oblique rotation method such as oblimin will be used, as the latent dimensions of teachers' knowledge of memory and learning processes are expected to be correlated.
Model fit will be evaluated using multiple indices.
For the purposes of the present study, models investigated through EFA and CFA will be considered to show acceptable fit when the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) is ≤ .08.
RMSEA values ≤ .06 will be interpreted as indicating particularly good fit, consistent with Hu and Bentler (1999).
text.formatted: RMSEA values ≤ .06 will be interpreted as indicating particularly good fit, consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Hu and Bentler (1999)</ref>.

text.text: Comparative fit index (CFI) and Tucker-Lewis index (TLI) values ≥ .95 will likewise be considered indicative of good fit, in line with Hu and Bentler (1999).

text.text: Standardized factor loadings will be examined to evaluate item relevance.
A standardized loading of ≥ .30 will be used as the prespecified criterion for adequate association between the item and the factor.
Items with loadings < .30 or substantial cross-loadings will be considered for revision or removal.

text.text: Decisions about item retention or removal will additionally take into account the theoretical alignment and content coverage of the items.
Cross-loadings will be considered substantial when an item shows factor loadings ≥ .30 on more than one factor.

After the form-specific structures have been investigated and cross-validated as described above, measurement invariance will be examined using a joint confirmatory factor analysis including both forms.
This analysis will be conducted only if the preceding analyses support substantively corresponding factor structures.
A schematic overview of the planned analytical procedure is provided in Figure 1.

text.text: The measurement invariance analysis will be conducted on the full sample after the factor structure and final set of retained items have been established.
We acknowledge that this approach does not provide a fully independent sample for the measurement invariance test.
However, the joint CFA is substantially more complex than the separate models because it includes both forms simultaneously as well as the residual covariances between matched item pairs.
Restricting this analysis to the confirmatory subsample would substantially reduce the available sample size and could compromise estimation stability.
If item removal during the preceding analyses results in the exclusion of one member of a conceptually matched pair, that pair will not contribute to the measurement invariance analysis.
Each form will be represented by its own latent factor or set of latent factors according to the structure retained in the preceding analyses, with corresponding latent factors allowed to correlate.

Because Original and Twin items are conceptually matched, a residual covariance will be specified a priori for each pair and freely estimated in both models to account for pair-specific covariance not explained by the latent factor(s).

Because item responses will be coded as binary indicators (0 = incorrect,1 = correct), measurement invariance will be evaluated using CFA with categorical indicators and the weighted least squares mean-and variance-adjusted estimator (WLSMV), following the measurement invariance framework described by Brown (2015).
text.formatted: Because item responses will be coded as binary indicators (0 = incorrect,1 = correct), measurement invariance will be evaluated using CFA with categorical indicators and the weighted least squares mean-and variance-adjusted estimator (WLSMV), following the measurement invariance framework described by <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Brown (2015)</ref>.

text.text: Two nested models will be estimated.

First, a baseline model will be specified in which the factor structure identified in the preceding analyses is modeled simultaneously for the Original and Twin forms, while the unstandardized factor loadings and indicator thresholds of corresponding items are freely estimated.

Second, a measurement invariance model will be estimated in which, for each retained matched pair, the unstandardized factor loading and indicator threshold of the Original item, are constrained to equal those of its Twin counterpart: λ Oi = λ Ti , τ Oi =τ Ti .
Here, λ and τ denote the unstandardized factor loading and the item threshold, respectively.
The subscripts O and T identify the Original and Twin forms, respectively, while i indexes the matched item pairs.
These equality constraints will be imposed only between matched Original and Twin items; parameters from different item pairs will not be constrained to equality.
The measurement invariance model will be compared with the baseline model using the robust chi-square difference test ( χ diff 2 ) appropriate for WLSMV.

Provided that the baseline and constrained models show acceptable overall fit, a non-significant difference test will be interpreted as evidence that constraining the factor loadings and indicator thresholds of corresponding Original and Twin items to equality does not produce a significant deterioration in model fit.
A significant difference test will be interpreted as evidence against full measurement invariance.
If full measurement invariance is not supported, modification indices will be inspected to identify noninvariant matched item pairs.
For a noninvariant item pair, the equality constraints on its factor loading and indicator threshold will be relaxed together.
The number and identity of noninvariant item pairs will be explicitly reported.

text.text: In this subsample, the probability of providing a correct response will be modeled as a function of years of teaching experience, level of tertiary qualification, and academic field.
Bachelor's degree will be the reference category for level of tertiary qualification, and non-psycho-pedagogical qualification the reference category for academic field.
Academic field will not be included in the full-sample model because it is not defined for participants without a tertiary qualification.
When the disciplinary classification of a qualification is not straightforward, it will be classified independently by two members of the research team.
Disagreements will be resolved through discussion before the outcome data are analyzed.
Because responses are nested within both participants and items, each model will include random intercepts for participants and items.
This approach will allow accounting for individual differences in overall response accuracy and for differences in item difficulty.
Fixed effects will be reported as log-odds coefficients and corresponding odds ratios (i.e., the exponentiated form of the same coefficients), together with 95% confidence intervals.

For continuous predictors and binary categorical predictors, statistical significance will be based on the p-value associated with the corresponding model coefficient, using two-sided tests with an alpha level of .05.

For categorical predictors with more than two levels, overall statistical significance will first be evaluated using likelihood-ratio tests; if the omnibus test is significant, specific model contrasts will then be evaluated using the same significance criterion.
As sensitivity analyses, both primary models will be reestimated including geographical area, school level, and sex as additional covariates.
The primary interpretation will be based on the corresponding unadjusted models, whereas the adjusted models will be interpreted as robustness checks.

Additional exploratory analyses will examine associations between item-level response accuracy and variables that are not included in the primary regression models and for which the available literature does not provide a sufficiently strong basis for directional a priori hypotheses.

These variables will include age, school level, subject area taught, geographical area, sex, the two self-reported knowledge ratings, cumulative hours of relevant non-university courses, the total number of peer-reviewed scientific articles read during the previous 12 months, and the number of those articles specifically concerning memory and learning processes.
Each exploratory association will be examined in a separate mixed-effects logistic regression model using the same item-level outcome and random-effects structure specified for the primary analyses.

Because research literature has provided contrasting evidence, it is not possible to specify directional hypotheses for these analyses, and their results will be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than as confirmatory evidence.

If a multidimensional structure is retained, Cronbach's alpha will be computed separately for each subscale, because alpha is most appropriate when items are intended to measure a single latent dimension.

We expect the exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses to provide evidence supporting the internal structure of both forms.
Given the exploratory nature of the initial stage and of the domain, no strict prediction is made regarding the exact number of factors that will emerge.

However, we expect EFA to identify theoretically interpretable factor solutions, characterized by coherent patterns of item loadings, limited cross-loadings, and a sufficient number of items loading substantially on the retained factor(s).

We further expect CFA, conducted on an independent subsample extracted from the same population, to support the adequacy of the corresponding solutions, with model fit indices falling within the good or optimal ranges defined in the Data Analysis section.
Overall, these results are expected to provide validity evidence based on internal structure.

If the form-specific analyses support substantively corresponding factor structures, we expect the joint CFA to support measurement invariance of the unstandardized factor loadings and indicator thresholds across matched Original and Twin items.
We also expect performance to be associated with the selected teacher background and educational variables.

Specifically, based on previous findings, we expect years of teaching experience to be negatively associated with the probability of providing a correct response, although this prediction is considered tentative because previous evidence is mixed.

In the full-sample model, we expect educational attainment to be associated with item-level accuracy, with participants holding higher completed educational qualifications generally showing a higher probability of responding correctly than participants whose highest qualification is an uppersecondary school diploma.

In the model restricted to participants with a tertiary qualification, we tentatively expect participants holding higher-level tertiary qualifications to show a higher probability of responding correctly than participants whose highest qualification is a bachelor's degree.
This prediction draws on findings concerning general pedagogical knowledge, although the reported advantage of higher qualifications is not consistent across countries (OECD, 2026).

text.text: We also expect participants whose highest tertiary qualification is in a psychological, pedagogical, educational, or closely related field to show a higher probability of responding correctly than participants whose tertiary qualification is in another disciplinary area.
Finally, we expect adequate internal consistency for both forms.

If a retained structure is unidimensional, Cronbach's alpha is expected to indicate adequate internal consistency for its total score according to the criterion specified in the Data Analysis section.

If a multidimensional structure is retained, Cronbach's alpha is expected to indicate adequate internal consistency for each subscale, while taking into account that shorter subscales may show lower alpha values.
These results will be interpreted together with the evidence on factor loadings, item content, and theoretical coverage of the construct.
